output:
**Subject: The building, and what you did**

Denis,

I have tried to write this email five times. Every time it came out half in French and half in words I don't want your kids to read. So I am going slowly, and I ask you to read it slowly too, to the end.

Last Thursday at 6 in the morning I was shaping the baguettes like every morning for 31 years. A man came into the bakery with a camera. He said he was from the agency, that he needed photos of the commercial space for the listing, and that "Mr. Denis" told him I was okay with it. I didn't understand at first. Then I understood. Karine had to take me in the back and make me sit down, because I was shaking and I was not nice to that man. It was not his fault. He was only doing what you told him.

After he left I went on Centris and there it was. Our building, papa's building, on rue Saint-Hubert, for $1,150,000. Photos of the apartments upstairs. The description said "excellent potential for redevelopment."

Denis, I learned that my brother was selling the building where I work from a stranger with a camera, before the sun was up, in front of my employee. Please think about that for one minute before you answer me.

I want to remind you of some things, because I think in Calgary maybe you forgot.

Papa bought that building in 1979. The bakery downstairs, two apartments up. Since maman died in February, it is half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August. Half of it is mine. Nobody puts it on the market without talking to me first, and nobody sells it without my signature.

After the funeral you called me. I remember exactly what you said, because I was so tired and it made me feel better. You said, "No rush, we decide together." Together. I believed you. I didn't push you, I didn't call you every week, I gave you time because I thought you were grieving too and you needed it.

In September I called you and told you clearly what I wanted to do. I want to buy your half. The caisse pre-approved me for $410,000. I know that is less than half of what the agent is asking. But we never even sat down to talk about the number. You never called me back to say "it's not enough," or "let's look at it," or anything. You just went quiet, and then you hired an agent and let him be the one to tell me.

That is the part I can't swallow. Not that you want money from the building. I understand you have your life, your house, your kids. I understand. But you didn't even call me. You sent a stranger to do it. Papa would have been ashamed, and you know it.

I also want to say this clearly, because I know what you think. You think I am sentimental. That I am attached to the old ovens and the smell and the memories, and that you are the one being practical. Okay, yes, I am sentimental, I will not lie. But this is business too, Denis. I have 6 employees. Karine has been with me 14 years. Some of my clients came in as kids with their parents and now they bring their own kids. That is 31 years of work, of getting up at 4 in the morning, of never taking a real vacation.

And I have always been a good tenant to the estate. I pay $2,400 every month. I was never late, not one time, not in 31 years. In 2019 when the roof had to be redone, I paid for it myself, $38,000, out of my own pocket, because maman didn't have it and I didn't want to bother you. I never asked anybody to pay me back. That roof is on the building you are selling now.

My lease finishes on April 30, 2027. You know who buys a building on Saint-Hubert for that price. It is a developer. They will tear it down for condos, or they will keep it and double my rent the day the lease ends. I cannot survive that. At 57 I cannot start again somewhere else. If the building goes to a developer, the bakery closes. It's that simple. Six people lose their job, and I lose the only thing I know how to do.

I keep thinking about when we were kids. Papa let you sleep in the back room with the flour sacks, remember? You loved it. You used to say it was the warmest room in Montreal. Maman would come looking for you at night and you would be asleep between the sacks, white all over like a little ghost. I still store the flour in that room. Every morning I walk past it. I don't say this to make you cry. I say it because that building is not only mine. It is yours too, your childhood is in there too, and I don't understand how you can sell it like a parking lot to a stranger, without even one phone call.

So here is what I am asking. It is not complicated.

1. Take the building off the market this week.
2. If you really cannot do that, then at the very least give me the first right to buy your half before any other offer is accepted, in writing. Let me make my offer properly, with my notary and the caisse, and let's talk about the price like brother and sister, not through agents.

I am ready to talk about the number. I am ready to look at how the roof counts, how the rent counts, what is fair. I am not asking for a gift. I am asking for a chance, and for respect.

And one more thing. I want you to answer me by phone. Your voice, not a text. I love your wife, and I know she reads English better than you and that she is probably reading this to you right now, and that's okay, bonjour. But this is between you and me. You owe me a phone call, Denis. After all of this, at least that.

I want you to understand that I am furious. I have not been this angry since I don't know when. I didn't sleep Thursday night, and I didn't sleep much since. But I am not writing to tell you I hate you, because I don't. You are my brother. Papa and maman are gone. It's only us now. I don't want to lose the building, but I don't want to lose you either. Please don't make me choose.

Call me. Any day this week, I'm at the bakery from 4 in the morning, you know where to find me. You always did.

[Your name]

---

A couple of things before you send it:

- I left the price gap in on purpose ($410,000 vs. about $575,000 for half at the asking price). Denis will see it anyway, so it's better to admit it yourself and say you're ready to talk than to look like you're hiding it.
- It's worth calling a notary this week, whatever Denis answers. In Quebec, when property is co-owned and one owner sells their share to an outsider, the other owner can sometimes buy that share back, but there are short deadlines. Your notary can tell you exactly where you stand, and you'll feel stronger on the phone with Denis if you know.
